extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, lawmakers, and legal theorists
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes normative principles governing the lawful limits, duties, and interactions of legislative, executive, and federative powers in a commonwealth (consent, property, promulgation, separation of powers, prerogative, and popular sovereignty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent of the society required for lawful lawmaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawful power of making laws requires the consent of the society; no body can make laws for a society without authority received from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All obedience ultimately terminates in the supreme power which the society consents to; oaths to foreign or subordinate powers cannot discharge a member from obedience to the legislative acting pursuant to the society's trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative power limited by what individuals had in the state of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative, even if supreme, cannot have more power than the persons who conferred it had in the state of nature; nobody can transfer more power than he has.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because a person in the state of nature has no arbitrary power over life or property of another, the legislative likewise cannot have arbitrary power to destroy life, liberty, or possessions; its power is limited to what was given for preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: End of government: preservation of mankind; laws must aim at public good
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative's power has no other end but the preservation of the society; laws must be limited to the public good and cannot justifiably destroy, enslave, or designedly impoverish the subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law of nature (preservation of mankind) is the fundamental rule; any human sanction contrary to it is not good or valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human laws must conform to law of nature and divine law
rubrics_metrics.description: Human laws are measured by higher rules — the law of God and the law of nature — and must not contradict them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If human laws contradict the law of nature or scripture, they are ill-made; obligations of natural law continue in society and may be given human penalties but not negated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws must be promulgated standing laws with known judges
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative is bound to dispense justice and decide rights by promulgated standing laws and known, authorized judges, not by extemporary arbitrary decrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without established laws and judges, natural law (unwritten) cannot consistently determine rights; otherwise every man would be judge, interpreter, and executioner in his own cause, producing disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Govern by established laws, not extemporary decrees
rubrics_metrics.description: Ruling by extemporary arbitrary decrees is inconsistent with the ends of society; governments ought to govern by declared and received laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extemporaneous, undetermined resolutions lead to uncertainty and allow rulers to employ power according to sudden thoughts, which is contrary to public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal application of the law (one rule for all statuses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws should not be varied in particular cases; they must have one rule for rich and poor, favorites at court and countrymen at plough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniform rules protect peace and security within the law's limits and keep rulers within bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative cannot take property without consent
rubrics_metrics.description: The supreme power cannot take any part of a man's property without his consent; property must be preserved as the end of government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If another can rightfully take your property at pleasure, you have no property; this includes arbitrary dispossession by prince, senate, or perpetual legislative body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxes and impositions require consent of the people
rubrics_metrics.description: It is fit that everyone who enjoys protection pay for it, but taxes must be with the consent of the majority, either directly or via their representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim to levy taxes without people's consent invades the fundamental law of property and subverts government’s end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative cannot transfer law-making power to others
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative, being a delegated power from the people, cannot pass the power to make laws to any other hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The people alone appoint the form of the commonwealth; the legislative's grant was only to make laws, not to make legislators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive must exist perpetually; legislative need not
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative need not always be in being (laws may be made in little time) but executive power must always exist to see to the execution of the laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separation of legislative and executive reduces temptation for those making laws to exempt themselves from obedience; a standing executive ensures continual enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federative power for external relations (war, peace, alliances)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a federative power distinct from the executive that manages controversies with those outside the commonwealth — war, peace, leagues, and alliances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federative matters are less amenable to antecedent standing laws and must largely be managed by the prudence and skill of those entrusted with them for the public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive and federative powers are distinct but often united
rubrics_metrics.description: Though conceptually distinct, executive and federative powers are almost always united in practice because both require the force of the society and continuous direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placing these forces in distinct, non-subordinate hands risks disorder and ruin; coordination is necessary to avoid conflicting commands.

rubrics_metrics.name: People retain supreme power to remove or alter legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the legislative is supreme while government subsists, the people retain a supreme power to remove or alter the legislative when it violates the trust for which it was instituted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All delegated power given with trust is limited by its end; when legislators neglect or oppose that end, the trust is forfeited and power reverts to those who granted it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convoking/dismissing legislature by executive is fiduciary, not supremacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive's power to assemble and dissolve the legislative is a fiduciary trust meant for the people's safety, not a grant of superiority over the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prerogative is to be exercised for public weal (e.g., calling assemblies when exigencies demand), and when abused (using force without authority), it is a state of war with the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of force without authority is a state of war
rubrics_metrics.description: If the executive uses the commonwealth's force to frustrate the legislative or acts without authority contrary to trust, that is to use force without authority and constitutes a state of war with the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such a state the people have a right to oppose and reinstate their legislative by force; opposing force with force is the remedy against unlawful aggression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation must remain proportionate and just
rubrics_metrics.description: Over time representation may become unequal and disproportionate; restoring true proportion to representation is legitimate and can be done for the public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where decay or custom has produced absurd representation (e.g., tiny decayed places sending as many representatives as populous counties), the rectification of representation in favor of fair proportion is a just prerogative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerogative: executive discretion to act for public good when law silent
rubrics_metrics.description: Prerogative is the executive's power to act by discretion for the public good where municipal law gives no direction, and sometimes even against it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because laws cannot foresee every accident (e.g., not tearing down an innocent's house to stop a fire next door), the executive may mitigate severity of law or pardon offenders when needed for preservation of the community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on commanders' power to seize private property
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where absolute authority over life and death is necessary (e.g., martial discipline), commanders cannot command soldiers to part with their goods; disciplinary power does not include disposal of a man's estate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a serjeant can order a soldier into danger but cannot command him to give one penny; generals can condemn to death but cannot seize a soldier's goods — property and command are distinct.
